# Designing for iOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. An iPhone experience must work both during brief checks on the move and through extended games, browsing, or media sessions. People switch among apps frequently. ## Best practices - Design for a medium-sized, dense display viewed at roughly 1–2 feet, usually held in one or both hands. Accommodate portrait and landscape use. - Keep primary content and actions clear, with secondary operations reachable through a small number of interactions rather than many simultaneous controls. - Support touch gestures, onscreen keyboards, and voice; use motion sensors, nearby spatial interactions, or personal information only where they improve the task. - Put frequent touch controls within comfortable reach, commonly the middle or lower display. Preserve swipe-back navigation and list-row gestures. - Adapt to orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type without breaking context. - With permission, use platform data and services to reduce typing: location, biometric authentication, and payments are examples. - Integrate appropriate system entry points: widgets, Home Screen quick actions, Spotlight search, Shortcuts, and activity views. Their familiar behavior helps people act outside the main app. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here.

# Designing for watchOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Apple Watch serves brief glances and focused actions while people are still or moving. The small, dense display is typically within about a foot when the wrist is raised. Always On also communicates when the wrist is lowered; many interactions last less than a minute. ## Best practices - Give the most useful information and action on a single glanceable screen, ideally requiring only one or two gestures. - Keep navigation shallow. Use the Digital Crown for vertical scrolling or moving among screens; support familiar taps, swipes, and drags. - Provide relevant actions through complications, notifications, Siri, and Shortcuts, which people may use more often than the app itself. - Use the Action button for a suitable essential action that can be performed without looking. - With appropriate access, personalize timely content using GPS, heart and blood-oxygen sensors, altitude, acceleration, and rotation data. - Make complications useful on every wrist raise and let a tap enter the right app context. Keep notifications timely, valuable, and actionable without requiring an app launch. - Use backgrounds and color to communicate supporting context and materials to clarify hierarchy and place. - Build an independently useful watch app that provides the extra detail and functionality beyond its notifications and complications. Integrate Always On and watch-face expectations. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 5, 2023.

This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Always On reduces brightness/motion while preserving glanceable information. The source describes Lock Screen widgets/Live Activities on iPhone 14 Pro/Pro Max, and the frontmost or background-session Watch app when the wrist lowers. Notifications can remain visible; a tap resumes active interaction. ## Best practices Redact private balances, health details, and sensitive notification content. Retain contextually useful personal information where expected, such as workout metrics or an arrival update; people can disable Always On. Keep primary information legible while dimming secondary detail/fills and simplifying rich images or large color areas. Maintain layout rather than removing controls; use unavailable appearances. Make infrequent subtle updates, such as scores instead of play-by-play, especially on a face-up phone visible peripherally. item.aggregated_output: # Widgets Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/widgets) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Anatomy](#Anatomy) - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Rendering modes](#Rendering-modes) - [Previews and placeholders](#Previews-and-placeholders) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) - [Specifications](#Specifications) Widgets provide timely information and focused actions outside the app. Contexts include phone/tablet Home and Lock Screens, Mac desktop/Notification Center, watch Smart Stack, spatial surfaces, and Apple HomeView. Choose size, location, and rendering behavior together. ## Anatomy WidgetKit supplies contextual treatment, but tailor the layout when a context needs a better information hierarchy. ### System family widgets Small commonly focuses on one fact, medium/large on more information/actions, extra large adds room where supported, and extra-large portrait is spatial-only. The supported-context matrix is factual source data: |Widget size |iPhone |iPad |Mac |Apple Vision Pro | |---------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------| |System small |Home Screen, Today View, StandBy, CarPlay, and Apple HomeView|Home Screen, Today View, and Lock Screen|Desktop and Notification Center|Horizontal and vertical surfaces| |System medium |Home Screen and Today View |Home Screen and Today View |Desktop and Notification Center|Horizontal and vertical surfaces| |System large |Home Screen and Today View |Home Screen and Today View |Desktop and Notification Center|Horizontal and vertical surfaces| |System extra large |Not supported |Home Screen and Today View |Desktop and Notification Center|Horizontal and vertical surfaces| |System extra large portrait|Not supported |Not supported |Not supported |Horizontal and vertical surfaces| ### Accessory widgets These compact families provide very limited information. Corner is watch-only; inline, circular, and rectangular also support phone/tablet Lock Screens as listed. |Widget size |iPhone |iPad |Apple Watch | |---------------------|-------------|-------------|------------------------------------------| |Accessory circular |Lock Screen |Lock Screen |Watch complications and in the Smart Stack| |Accessory corner |Not supported|Not supported|Watch complications | |Accessory inline |Lock Screen |Lock Screen |Watch complications | |Accessory rectangular|Lock Screen |Lock Screen |Watch complications and in the Smart Stack| ### Appearances Widgets can be full color, tinted monochrome, or clear/translucent. Home Screens can use light/dark, desaturated tint, or clear Liquid Glass. visionOS adds physical framing and glass/paper treatment, with palette tint choices. Lock Screen accessories desaturate; StandBy and HomeView Modular remove backgrounds and scale content, using red monochrome in low light. A watch rectangular accessory can be full color/tinted on a face or live in Smart Stack. Rendering mode varies by context rather than following one universal rule. |Platform |Full-color |Accented |Vibrant | |----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------| |iPhone |Home Screen, Today view, StandBy and CarPlay (with the background removed)|Home Screen and Today view |Lock Screen, StandBy in Night Mode| |iPad |Home Screen and Today view |Home Screen and Today view |Lock Screen | |Apple Watch |Smart Stack, complications |Smart Stack, complications |Not supported | |Mac |Desktop and Notification Center |Not supported |Desktop | |Apple Vision Pro|Horizontal and vertical surfaces |Horizontal and vertical surfaces |Not supported | |Apple HomeView |Home Screen, Modular face (with the background removed) |Home Screen, Modular face (with the background removed)|Modular face in Night Mode | ## Best practices Choose a simple purpose central to the app and useful changing information. A static app-icon replica offers little benefit. Use multiple sizes only when they add layers of useful information, not stretched copies. Balance immediate clarity with secondary details available on longer inspection. Keep larger variants on the same core purpose. Brand through restrained color/type/glyphs; if source attribution needs a logo, a small upper-trailing mark suffices. Offer configuration when people must choose their content; otherwise useful automatic recents can remove setup. Avoid lookalike widget elements inside the app that behave differently. Explain any signed-in functionality when logged out. A subtle occasion-specific visual treatment can add delight without losing utility. ### Updating widget content Widgets refresh periodically under system limits rather than continuously. Match updates to meaningful changes and expected viewing, adding freshness text when data can age between checks. Use system date/time views to preserve reload budget. Show available data promptly instead of replacing it with placeholders while refreshing. Standard/custom transitions of up to 2 seconds can reveal new data. ### Adding interactivity Ordinary widget activation opens the app; native buttons/toggles can do simple relevant work in place. Deep-link precisely to the selected content. Keep targets clear and glanceable instead of recreating a miniature app. Inline accessories have one tap target. ### Choosing margins and padding Supply adaptable content and let system sizing handle device scale; iPad can render a larger canvas before downscaling. Most widgets use 16-pt margins; 11 pt can suit tighter grouped graphics/buttons/background shapes. Mac desktop and Lock Screen/StandBy use smaller contextual margins. Use container-relative rounding so inset shapes align with the outer corners. ### Displaying text in widgets Prefer system text styles and aligned SF Symbols. Custom type should be sparse and readable, often limited to large text with SF Pro for small labels. Generally keep type at least 11 pt. Render actual text rather than rasterizing so scaling and VoiceOver work. In iOS, iPadOS, and visionOS, SwiftUI system/custom fonts support Dynamic Type Large through AX5. ### Using color Use color to support content rather than compete with it, and provide noncolor meaning because tinting, grayscale, and watch-face inversion can change the result. Widget editing colors can come from the asset catalog. Preserving full-color images in clear/tinted modes can overpower system customization; reserve it for meaningful media such as artwork and keep images smaller than the whole widget where appropriate. ## Rendering modes ### Full-color Support light/dark through semantic colors or asset variants, normally matching light backgrounds to light appearance and dark to dark. ### Accented Separate primary and accent groups. The system applies context-dependent solid colors; watch uses white for primary and the selected watch-face color for accent. Preserve hierarchy across all tint/clear options. The source's platform table excludes accented Mac mode while one prose sentence mentions Mac group tinting; do not infer Mac support from that conflicting sentence. ### Vibrant Pixel opacity controls how much background material passes through, while grayscale brightness determines visual emphasis. Use opaque white/light gray for prominent information and darker opaque grays for supporting details. Check grayscale contrast; varying white opacity is not a substitute for optimized grayscale values. ## Previews and placeholders Gallery previews should show realistic real or simulated data promptly and accurately represent each variant. Loading placeholders can preserve static framing and use semitransparent blocks for dynamic text or images. Describe the widget with an approachable sentence-case action verb, omitting filler about adding/using a widget. Group its sizes under one description. The gallery Add button can use an appropriate brand color. ## Platform considerations No additional macOS rules are specified. Widgets are unsupported in tvOS. ### iOS, iPadOS Treat Lock Screen widgets like complications: useful data first, with inline above the clock and circular/rectangular below. Verify reduced-luminance Always On grayscale. For frequent real-time bounded updates, design a Live Activity, reusing appropriate components rather than expecting widget refreshes to behave continuously. #### StandBy and CarPlay StandBy shows two scaled small-family widgets; CarPlay also scales that family with removable backgrounds. Use large readable information and restrained rich imagery, especially for across-room or driving glances. Mark backgrounds removable. Test red monochrome in low-light StandBy. #### Apple HomeView Small-family widgets can appear on a shared Modular face and personalized Home Screens, sourced locally or from connected household iPhones/iPads. The household has one Modular face with up to four widgets, potentially exposing one person's calendar to others. Each enrolled member has their own Home Screen; consider the privacy difference. ### visionOS Widgets persist on horizontal/vertical surfaces through device restarts at consistent real-world scale. Full color is default; selected palette tints use accented mode. Elevated frames have customizable widths, and widget-specific themes can exist despite no global light/dark appearance. Design as room objects, from desk information to wall posters, and test all palettes and lighting, including elements excluded from tinting. #### Thresholds and sizes Design nearby/default and distant/simplified versions. At a distance, enlarge type, reduce detail, and remove controls; retain common elements across thresholds for continuity. Match family size to the likely surface. People can scale to 75–125%, so use clear hierarchy and high-resolution assets readable across distances. #### Mounting styles Elevated is default and works on walls and horizontal surfaces, tilting back on desks and casting a grounding shadow. Recessed sets content into vertical surfaces only, suitable for ambient/windowlike content. Opt out of unsuitable styles; recessed-only widgets cannot be placed horizontally. Mounting support applies per configuration, so separate configurations when variants need different support. Test every elevated frame width because layout cannot adapt to the selected frame. #### Treatment styles Paper provides a solid print-like object whose whole appearance follows ambient brightness. Glass separates foreground and background: important foreground stays bright/full color while supporting material adapts to lighting. Choose paper for artwork/posters and glass for information needing reliable contrast. ### watchOS Smart Stack backgrounds default black; a meaningful custom color can communicate state. Supply relevance based on location or current system activity to encourage timely display/placement. ## Specifications Use these factual dimensions as design guidance and keep production layouts flexible. # Live Activities Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/live-activities) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Anatomy](#Anatomy) - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Presentation](#Presentation) - [CarPlay](#CarPlay) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) - [Specifications](#Specifications) Live Activities track a bounded task or event through frequent updates over a few hours. They begin on iPhone or iPad and can appear on the Lock/Home Screen, Dynamic Island and StandBy, paired Mac menu bar, Apple Watch Smart Stack, and CarPlay Dashboard. ## Anatomy Support compact, minimal, expanded, and Lock Screen presentations. The system composes these for available space and devices. ### Compact A single Dynamic Island activity uses separate leading/trailing elements around the TrueDepth camera. ### Minimal Multiple activities use compact circular/oval treatments, up to three where supported: one attached and others detached. Tap opens the app; hold expands. ### Expanded Holding compact/minimal content reveals a larger presentation. ### Lock Screen A bottom banner uses a layout related to expanded. On devices without Dynamic Island, essential update alerts can briefly overlay this banner on Home or another app. ### StandBy Minimal content expands on tap to a Lock Screen layout scaled 2×. A custom background extends across the screen. ## Best practices Use tasks with clear starts and ends, ideally no more than 8 hours. Show only immediately useful information, with details in the app. Exclude ads and promotions. Avoid exposed sensitive content; summarize or redact and offer app access/configuration. Match app identity across appearances; a logo mark can appear without a container, but do not use the full app icon. Do not draw attention to Dynamic Island from inside the app. Use legible large text, generally medium weight or stronger. ### Creating Live Activity layouts Adapt to actual screens and scale factors. Keep layout only as large as content needs. For limited-width Dynamic Island contexts, fit compact/minimal content within a 28-pt circle with abbreviations or graphics; use leading-only when a meaningful trailing version cannot fit. Favor familiar templates, even concentric margins, and container-relative corner radii. Inset groups or use a thick dividing line instead of extending content to edges. A blurred drawing-tool preview can help align angular content within rounded corners. Adjust Lock Screen/expanded height as available information grows or shrinks. ### Choosing colors Only Lock Screen permits custom background colors; compact, minimal, and expanded backgrounds are system-controlled. Dynamic Island is opaque black, so meaningful bold foreground color can express identity. Match its dark-background keyline to related content. Check custom Lock Screen contrast in both appearances and reduced-luminance Always On. ### Adding transitions and animating content updates Animations can last at most 2 seconds and are not played in reduced-luminance Always On. Use numeric changes, fades, scale, or movement to explain updates. Preserve existing elements as layout grows rather than removing/readding everything. Avoid transition collisions; animate a moved item and fade other list elements when needed. ### Offering interactivity Deep-link to the relevant task. Favor one essential button or toggle for a direct action, pause/resume, or response to meaningful progress, preserving space for status and reducing accidental activation. ### Starting, updating, and ending a Live Activity Begin at expected moments, including automatic starts for followed events, with an easy opt-out in the corresponding app view. Offer an App Shortcut when useful. Update only for changed content. Alert only for crucial updates and avoid a parallel push for the same information. Prefer one dynamically changing activity for related simultaneous events. End immediately when the task ends: Dynamic Island/CarPlay remove it, while Lock Screen, Mac, and watch can retain it for up to 4 hours. Choose a shorter useful summary lifetime, commonly 15–30 minutes, proportional to the activity. ## Presentation Design the iPhone presentations first, then tailor layouts for StandBy, watch, and driving while supporting every destination. ### Compact presentation Show essential changing data. Make both halves read as one through coherent color/type and balanced widths. Fit snugly against the camera without extra inner padding or unnecessary status-bar obstruction; shorten units or precision as needed. Both halves should deep-link to the same relevant app screen. ### Minimal presentation Preserve recognition while conveying current information instead of only a static logo. ### Expanded presentation Expand predictably from the smaller layout, retaining relative positions and fitting content close to the camera rather than leaving unused gaps. ### Lock Screen presentation Create a distinct task layout rather than copying notification structure. Use restrained tint/background customization to fit personalized wallpapers. Verify contrast in both appearances and Always On, including the system-generated dismiss-button color; override its foreground if needed. Standard margins are 14 pt, with tighter spacing only when content grouping needs it. ### StandBy presentation Supply assets and, where useful, a custom layout for the larger scale. The default background blends with the bezel and surroundings and permits slightly more content scale. Preserve margins so expansion does not crop graphics, and test the red-tinted Night Mode. ## CarPlay The default combines compact halves. A supplemental small family can support larger type and more information. Its custom layout is also used on watch, but CarPlay disables buttons and toggles; driving-oriented activities should prioritize timely content over those controls. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS or iPadOS rules are specified. Live Activities are unsupported in tvOS and visionOS. ### macOS Paired Mac menu-bar presentations use compact/minimal/expanded styles. Activation opens the app through iPhone Mirroring. ### watchOS The activity appears atop the paired watch's Smart Stack, combining compact halves by default. Tap opens a watch app when available; otherwise it opens a full-screen view with a paired-iPhone launch button. A custom layout can improve essential progress, changes, and controls, but consider its shared use in CarPlay where interaction is disabled. ## Specifications These source dimensions are design guidance in points; Watch faces choose supported families for their slots. ## Best practices Prioritize useful changing information over a static app launcher. Support every family where possible, falling back to a recognizable launch image when useful data cannot fit. Tinted mode desaturates full-color content and applies the selected watch color; retain meaning without color alone and provide alternate tinted images if needed. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Privacy Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Communicate collection and usage clearly and protect granted data. Keep App Store privacy disclosures accurate for new releases and updates; people rely on them before downloading. ## Best practices Collect only what the specific feature requires and make access as precise as possible. Respect Hide My Email, Mail Privacy Protection, and tracking choices. Prefer on-device processing, including Create ML/Neural Engine where useful, to avoid unnecessary server transfers. Use system encryption, key management, and established security protections, including CloudKit’s additional encrypted data types where available. ## Requesting permission Protected categories include personal/location/health/financial/contact information, user-created content, messages/calendar/music/gameplay/HomeKit data, media, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/local network resources, camera/microphone, the advertising identifier, and permission-gated ARKit data in a visionOS Full Space. The system displays the app’s purpose string and stores choices/descriptions in privacy settings. Ask when the person invokes the relevant feature. Request at launch only when access is essential and obviously necessary, such as location for navigation or room information for a spatial game that needs walls. Write a short, specific, active, complete sentence in sentence case with a period, explaining both use and reason. Vague promises of a better experience and commands to enable access do not explain the need. ### Pre-alert screens, windows, or views Usually context explains the request. If extra explanation is essential, use one button clearly leading to the system alert, such as Continue/Next; do not label it Allow or mimic the actual consent choice. Do not add cancellation, close, or other actions except those needed for legal consent. These restrictions apply to pre-permission custom explanations, not ordinary unrelated onboarding screens. ### Tracking requests Show the AppTrackingTransparency alert before collecting tracking information, including if tracking begins at launch. Do not offer incentives, imitate a permission prompt, display an image of the alert, annotate behind it, or otherwise manipulate rushed choices. Such patterns can cause App Review rejection. A legally required consent view before/after the system alert is permitted by the source’s stated review guidance. ## Location button On iOS/iPadOS/watchOS, the system location button provides one-time access at the task’s moment of need. The first tap teaches and confirms its behavior through a system alert; later taps grant access without repeating that education. Authorization expires when app use ends. With no prior status it resembles Allow Once; an existing While Using status is unchanged. Use it for individual tasks such as attaching a location or finding a nearby item/store. Customize only the supplied title, filled/outline glyph, foreground/background colors, and corner radius. Keep all localized and accessibility-size text untruncated and maintain contrast/transparency limits. Persistent customization violations can prevent location access even though the button still triggers other app actions. ## Protecting data Prefer passkeys; if passwords remain, add two-factor verification. Use Face ID, Optic ID, or Touch ID to protect continued signed-in access where appropriate. Store secrets in the encrypted keychain, never plaintext files even with restrictive permissions. Prefer established authentication, Sign in with Apple, and Password AutoFill over invented schemes. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS/tvOS/watchOS rules are listed. ### macOS Sign externally distributed apps with a valid Developer ID. Use sandboxing to limit resource/data access; Mac App Store apps require it. Account for fast user switching rather than assuming the current person is the only signed-in account. ### visionOS System ARKit algorithms support lighting, mapping, persistence, segmentation, and related rendering in Shared Space without exposing raw data to apps. ARKit API access requires Full Space, and plane estimation, scene reconstruction, image anchoring, and hand tracking require permission. Gaze remains private: system hover feedback can respond before a tap without disclosing where someone looks. Compatibility back-camera input is blank; front-camera input represents spatial Personas with permission. Adapt imported phone/tablet camera-dependent features by removal or content import instead of assuming conventional camera capture. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 21, 2023.

People switch among apps frequently. ## Best practices - Design for a medium-sized, dense display viewed at roughly 1–2 feet, usually held in one or both hands. Accommodate portrait and landscape use. - Keep primary content and actions clear, with secondary operations reachable through a small number of interactions rather than many simultaneous controls. - Support touch gestures, onscreen keyboards, and voice; use motion sensors, nearby spatial interactions, or personal information only where they improve the task. - Put frequent touch controls within comfortable reach, commonly the middle or lower display. Preserve swipe-back navigation and list-row gestures. - Adapt to orientation, Dark Mode, and Dynamic Type without breaking context. - With permission, use platform data and services to reduce typing: location, biometric authentication, and payments are examples. - Integrate appropriate system entry points: widgets, Home Screen quick actions, Spotlight search, Shortcuts, and activity views. # Designing for watchOS Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. Apple Watch serves brief glances and focused actions while people are still or moving. The small, dense display is typically within about a foot when the wrist is raised. Always On also communicates when the wrist is lowered; many interactions last less than a minute. ## Best practices - Give the most useful information and action on a single glanceable screen, ideally requiring only one or two gestures. - Keep navigation shallow. Use the Digital Crown for vertical scrolling or moving among screens; support familiar taps, swipes, and drags. - Provide relevant actions through complications, notifications, Siri, and Shortcuts, which people may use more often than the app itself. - Use the Action button for a suitable essential action that can be performed without looking. - With appropriate access, personalize timely content using GPS, heart and blood-oxygen sensors, altitude, acceleration, and rotation data. - Make complications useful on every wrist raise and let a tap enter the right app context. Keep notifications timely, valuable, and actionable without requiring an app launch. - Use backgrounds and color to communicate supporting context and materials to clarify hierarchy and place. - Build an independently useful watch app that provides the extra detail and functionality beyond its notifications and complications. Integrate Always On and watch-face expectations. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-watchos) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 5, 2023.
